Chapter Two: Inside the Organization — Daily Life in Intelligence.
You know, life inside a security agency is nothing like what most people imagine from the outside. We’ve all seen those stereotypes—tough agents, fearless, holding absolute power. But honestly, the truth is a lot more complicated.
Picture this: behind closed doors, surrounded by piles of files, these officers are living double lives. There’s this delicate balance—strength and vulnerability, feeling in control but also, sometimes, afraid.
The day starts early, usually with a routine morning meeting. Everyone sits around a long table, exchanging cautious glances. Trust? It’s never absolute. Even the lightest jokes come with hidden messages. I remember one time, someone tried to break the tension with a joke about the daily grind. But instead of laughter, there were these quick, nervous looks—almost as if people were wondering, “Was that joke really just a joke?”
Daily work? It covers everything from gathering intel, to writing reports, to monitoring suspects. One day, an officer is sent to watch a government employee who might be sympathetic to the opposition. It’s not easy. Surveillance takes patience, precision, and—maybe hardest of all—hiding your feelings. At night, he comes home exhausted, weighed down by guilt. Still, he tells himself this is just part of the job, and everyone else is doing the same thing.
Inside the agency, the hierarchy is strict. Orders come from the top. There’s no room for debate or objection. I’ll never forget the story of an officer who was ordered to frame someone for a crime. He didn’t believe it was right, but he couldn’t say no. In that moment, he felt like just a tool in a much bigger system. Many justify it by saying, “I’m just following orders,” but deep down, that doesn’t erase the guilt.
Relationships between colleagues are tricky, too. There’s this hidden rivalry for promotions and rewards. Everyone tries to show loyalty to the leadership. One day, a man noticed his close friend started avoiding him, acting more reserved. Later, he found out that his friend had actually been assigned to watch him. That’s when it hit him—trust is a rare currency here, and everyone lives in a constant circle of suspicion.
Life outside work isn’t any easier. In markets and cafés, security officers sense they’re being watched, too. People eye them cautiously, some avoid talking altogether. At one family gathering, an officer noticed his relatives were suddenly more guarded, as if afraid their words might be reported. That feeling of isolation only grows over time, making personal life even harder.
Still, there are moments of real humanity. One day, two colleagues shared a quiet break together, talking about their old dreams—who they were before joining intelligence. For a moment, the conversation was genuine, free of suspicion. It felt like they’d stepped back into their former lives, and realized they still held onto a small piece of their humanity, despite everything.
And that’s how life goes inside intelligence: strict orders, constant suspicion, and the struggle to hold onto some shred of your own humanity. Every day brings fresh challenges and leaves a mark that’s hard to erase.
